case_name: Burrell v. Regional Municipality of Peel Police Services Board
text:
COURT
FILE NO.:
01-CV-211652

DATE
OF MOTION:
September 25, 2007

ENDORSEMENT
RELEASED:
November 2, 2007

SUPERIOR COURT OF
JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
EMLIN
BURRELL v. THE REGIONAL MUNICIPALITY OF PEEL POLICE SERVICES BOARD, CHIEF OF
POLICE NOEL CATNEY, PLOICE SERGEANT CONROY, POLICE CONSTABLE K. GRAHAM and
POLICE CONSTABLE R. KETT

BEFORE:
Master
R. Dash

COUNSEL:
Ernest Guiste, for the
plaintiff

Maria Kotsopoulos, for the
defendants

REASONS FOR DECISION

[
1
]

This is a motion by the defendants to dismiss,
or alternatively stay, the action for failure to pay two costs orders pursuant
to rules 57.03(2) and 60.12. Neither cost order had been appealed. Two motions
were heard to vary the costs orders, one before Brown J. and one before me.
Both were unsuccessful. The plaintiff is impecunious and she raises issues of
access to justice. Much has been written lately about impecuniosity as a factor
in determining whether to award costs against a person without means to pay the
award. The plaintiff’s impecuniosity was considered at the time that the awards
were made. I am now asked to consider whether it is just to dismiss or stay the
action notwithstanding her impecuniosity.

[
2
]

A balance must be struck between on the one hand
the rights of an indigent litigant to have his or her day in court without
concern that access thereto will be denied because of unpaid interlocutory
costs orders and on the other hand the rights of other litigants not to be
faced with litigants who, using impecuniosity as a shield against the costs
consequences of their actions, are free to ignore the rules and orders of the
court.

[
3
]

As I have decided that it is appropriate in all
the circumstances to stay the action until at least the first costs order is
paid, it is important that I set out the sorry history of this action that led
to the two costs orders and the events that followed the two orders.

EVENTS PRIOR TO THE FIRST DISMISSAL
MOTION

[
4
]

The action was commenced on May 29, 2001. The
plaintiff claimed damages for assault, negligence, false arrest, false
imprisonment, breach of fiduciary duty and breach of charter rights arising out
of an incident on November 29, 2000 during an investigation regarding the
plaintiff’s son. The named defendants were the Peel Regional Police and three
police officers. The plaintiff was originally representing herself in this
action, but on January 29, 2004 a notice of appointment of solicitor was served
by solicitor Leslyn Lewis. There were several Call-Over
Court appearances. Examinations for discovery were
conducted of the plaintiff on December 7 and 8, 2004. Numerous undertakings
were given, some of which required the plaintiff to provide information or
documents and other undertakings required execution of authorizations to allow
the defendant to obtain non-party records. In the interim, on December 2, 2004,
a trial date was set on consent for February 6, 2006. The action then proceeded
to mediation on October 7, 2005 and pre-trial conference on November 9, 2005.
Undertakings were still outstanding and lists of undertakings were sent to Ms.
Lewis on October 6, 2005 and on December 5, 2005, together with authorizations
to be signed.

[
5
]

By mid November, solicitor-client relations had
broken down between the plaintiff and Ms. Lewis and on November 17, 2005 she
provided a summary of the file to Ernest Guiste, the plaintiff’s current
lawyer. Mr. Guiste says he took on the file in reliance upon Ms. Lewis’s
representation to him that there were no outstanding undertakings. Ms. Lewis
turned over the file to Mr. Guiste on December 7, 2005 and on the same date Mr.
Guiste served his notice of change of solicitors. Mr. Guiste described Ms.
Lewis’s file as “a mess”. It does not appear that Ms. Lewis had received the
December 5 letter from the defendant with the authorizations by the time she
turned over the file to Mr. Guiste, nor did she pass them on to Mr. Guiste. On
December 12, 2005 Mr. Mazzuca, the defendants’ solicitor, sent to Mr. Guiste a
copy of the December 5 letter to Ms. Lewis, but apparently without the
authorizations.

[
6
]

Any misapprehensions that Mr. Guiste had about
undertakings being complete would have been cleared up on January 4, 2006 when
he was served with the defendant’s motion to compel answers to undertakings
returnable January 10, 2006. The undertakings were set out in a schedule and
there were references to the transcript. On January 9, 2006 Mr. Guiste attended
a To-Be-Spoken-To Court and obtained an adjournment of the trial scheduled for
February 6, 2006 as he had only recently been retained and he was understandably
not ready for trial. At that time examinations of the defendants were
incomplete and amendments to the statement of claim were being considered. A
new trial date was set on consent for November 13, 2006, over 10 months away.

[
7
]

Meanwhile, the defendant’s motion to compel
undertakings was adjourned on the basis of Mr. Guiste’s agreement to answer
outstanding undertakings by April 30, 2006. None were answered and it does not
appear that any efforts were made to answer them or even to ascertain what the
undertakings were. Further copies of the list of undertakings were sent to Mr.
Guiste several times. As a result the motion came on before Master Clark on
June 27, 2006. Mr. Guiste consented to an order to answer the undertakings by
August 3, 2006 and to pay $250 in costs. The undertakings were set out in a
chart attached to the motion record and were referred to in the order.

[
8
]

In the interim, in July 2006, defendant’s
counsel sent to Mr. Guiste a copy of the authorizations that were previously
sent to Ms. Lewis. Mr. Guiste took no steps between Master Clark’s order on
June 27 and the deadline of August 3, to answer undertakings, except to have
the authorizations signed. There is no evidence that he even looked at what was
required by the undertakings. In fact 24 undertakings remained outstanding that
could not be answered by the authorizations as well as 5 continuing
undertakings. The costs ordered by Master Clark went unpaid.

THE FIRST DISMISSAL MOTION AND THE
FIRST COSTS ORDER

[
9
]

As a result, the defendant brought a motion to
dismiss the action for failure to comply with Master Clark’s order and failure
to answer undertakings returnable before me on August 11, 2006. Mr. Guiste
argued that the authorizations were now signed and he believed undertakings
were answered. He requested an adjournment to file responding material, obtain
an affidavit from Ms. Lewis or examine her under rule 39.03 and cross-examine
Mr. Mazzuca on his affidavit. I noted:

There are other allegedly outstanding undertakings not
dependent on the authorizations and Mr. Guiste “believes” they have been
answered, but has no proof they have been answered with him today despite the
list of undertakings being in his possession since January. The time to argue
whether undertakings were outstanding should have been before Master Clark, but
the plaintiff consented to an order to answer them. He also questions whether
the undertakings were given, as he has no transcript.

I noted that the plaintiff should have
an opportunity to put in responding material “presumably an affidavit from the
plaintiff herself or from Ms. Lewis outlining when various undertakings were
answered.” I adjourned the motion to September 28, 2006 and extended the time
for payment of the $250 costs ordered by Master Clark to August 25, 2006.

[
10
]

The plaintiff then brought a motion to amend the statement of claim,
compel further documents and discovery from the defendants and transfer the
action to case management returnable August 25, 2006 before Master Graham. Mr.
Guiste also sought a stay of my order compelling the payment by August 25 of
the costs ordered by Master Clark. Master Graham refused the request to stay my
order and adjourned the remainder of the motion to be heard by me together with
the defendant’s motion to dismiss on September 28.

[
11
]

Both motions came back on before me on September 28, 2006. It was
then less than seven weeks before the second trial date consented to by Mr.
Guiste. He indicated he would be attending a To-Be-Spoken-To Court to request
another adjournment because he was not ready for trial. Mr. Guiste filed an
affidavit from Ms. Lewis in which she confirmed her belief that when Mr. Guiste
took over the file in November 2005 undertakings were answered, however she did
not have the benefit of a transcript at the time. No evidence whatsoever was
filed to demonstrate that the undertakings had in fact been answered. There had
still been no attempt to answer any of the undertakings except to have the
authorizations signed. I held there were still 24 outstanding undertakings that
could not be satisfied by signing the authorizations and five continuing
undertakings, to which there had yet to be any response despite the trial being
seven weeks away.

[
12
]

Mr. Guiste claimed that when he appeared before Master Clark on June
27, 2006 he believed that undertakings were answered and there were only a few
loose ends to tie up. Mr. Guiste however had not looked at the file to confirm
whether the undertakings had been answered prior to consenting to the order,
and was still relying on Ms. Lewis’s statement made in November 2005. I asked
Mr. Guiste why he consented to an order to answer specified undertakings by
August 3 if he believed all undertakings had been answered. I recorded his
answer in my reasons on that date as follows:

Mr. Guiste says he was in a hurry to watch a televised
soccer match and so consented to the order in the mistaken belief that
undertakings were answered and there were only a few loose ends to tie up. I
have no evidence to that effect but the explanation defies belief. A lawyer
does not consent to answer specified and listed undertakings if he believed
they were answered. Further, even if he consented in order to give him time to
see what was truly outstanding, there is no evidence of efforts made between
Master Clark’s order on June 27 and the August 3 deadline, other than executing
the authorizations provided.

[
13
]

As of the September 28 appearance before me, Mr. Guiste had still
not looked at the undertakings to see if they were answered, let alone answer
them. I held as follows:

Mr. Guiste has had the file since December 7, 2005 and
it is clear to me that little or nothing has been done by him to comply with
undertakings, to ascertain from Ms. Lewis’ files whether undertakings were
answered, or otherwise to prepare for the trial first scheduled for February 6,
2006 and now scheduled for November 13, 2006.

It is my view that since Mr. Guiste took on the case,
whatever the expectations on November 17, 2005, he had the responsibility to
comply with his client’s undertakings and with Master Clark’s order. He has
known of the outstanding undertakings since January 4, 2006. I appreciate Mr.
Guiste is a sole practitioner and has other files, but there is no excuse for
failing to give this file any reasonable degree of attention over the past 10
months…

There is absolutely no acceptable excuse for not
complying with undertakings. There is absolutely no excuse for failing to
comply with a consent order of the court. I have no evidence of ANY steps
having been taken to comply except to have authorizations signed.

[
14
]

I referred to the following quote from
Cossette v. Gojit
[1]
as applicable to the matter
before me:

He has
shown a cavalier attitude to orders of the court and to his responsibilities as
a litigant. He complies as and when it suits him, typically long after
court-imposed deadlines and at the 11th hour when faced with a motion to
dismiss. A litigant should not have to bring a series of motions to dismiss in
order to advance the litigation and cause the defaulting party to do what has
been ordered.

[
15
]

The defendant urged that I dismiss the action since there was no
apparent attempt to comply with Master Clark’s order. I concluded as follows:

If a party were permitted to continue without
complying with the court’s orders, the conduct would go unsanctioned and the
court would lose all pretence of control over the party’s conduct.

Given the total lack of attempt to comply, I would be
justified in dismissing, not only under rule 60.12, but also under rule 34.15
given rule 31.07(1)(c) which deems a failure to answer undertakings within 60
days as a failure to answer a question.

Notwithstanding all of the above, dismissal is an
extreme remedy. Ms. Burrell should not be prejudiced by the default of Ms.
Lewis and then of Mr. Guiste except as a last resort. We have now come to the
door of last resort. The plaintiff shall have one final opportunity to comply
with her undertakings…If there is a failure to comply, the action will be
dismissed on the return date.

I therefore adjourned the motion to
October 19 and ordered compliance with specific undertakings by October 12,
2006. Costs were reserved to the October 19 hearing. The plaintiff’s motion to
amend was also adjourned to October 19.

[
16
]

Prior to the return of the motion, the parties attended a
To-Be-Spoken-To Court before Echlin J. to deal with the plaintiff’s request for
a further adjournment of the fixed trial date. Mr. Guiste submitted that he
needed an adjournment to amend the statement of claim, deliver a defence to
counterclaim (which had never been done despite a counterclaim delivered years
earlier), complete examinations for discovery and serve an expert’s report.
Echlin J. vacated the November 13 trial date, transferred the action to the
long trials list, set a deadline for the plaintiff to provide draft amended
pleadings and ordered that all future examinations for discovery of the
defendants be in writing. Written interrogatories were ordered to be provided
by December 29, 2006 “failing which there shall be no further right to any additional
interrogatories by the plaintiff” and the plaintiff was to provide the name of
her proposed expert and serve copies of the expert’s report by February 28,
2007. The costs before Echlin J. were reserved to me to be determined with the
other matters scheduled for October 19.

[
17
]

Prior to the return of the defendant’s motion to dismiss, Mr. Guiste
had retained another solicitor, Shedrack Agbakwa, to respond to the outstanding
undertakings and attend on October 19.  The motion came back on before me on
October 19. Mr. Agbakwa had taken matters in hand and I determined that “the
plaintiff has now substantially complied with her undertakings and the
defendant is no longer seeking a dismissal.” I ordered the few remaining
undertakings by a certain date.

[
18
]

The defendants sought their costs of the motion. The plaintiff
argued that costs be reserved until after trial because of the plaintiff’s
impecuniosity. I ordered that the plaintiff pay the defendant’s costs within 30
days fixed in the sum of $5000. My endorsement as to costs was as follows:

The sorry history of this matter is outlined in my
endorsements of August 11 and September 28, 2006.  It is clear that since Mr.
Guiste's involvement in December 2005, he made absolutely no effort to answer
undertakings, clearly outlined for him in the January 2006 motion record.  He
consented to the order of Master Clark yet made no effort to comply with it.
The August 11 adjournment was granted to allow him time to see what needed to
be done and put in responding material.  Nothing was done to comply with or
even examine the undertakings - the only issue addressed was the
authorizations.  His failure to deal with this file resulted in two trial
adjournments because he was not ready, most recently on October 2 before
Echlin, J.  The defendant has incurred expenses of $13,884 on this motion
including the 3 attendances before me and the attendance before Echlin, J.,
which he reserved to me.  The costs claim would be approximately $10,000 on a
partial indemnity scale.  The defendants claim $5,000. That is a fair and
reasonable amount in the circumstances.

The plaintiff asks for no costs or for costs to be
deferred until after trial because she is impecunious and on social
assistance.  As stated in
Stacey v Barrie Yacht Club
,
[2003] OJ No. 4171

and similar cases, allowing a plaintiff to set up her own impoverishment as a
shield against costs sanctions would allow her to disobey court orders with
impunity.  I agree with plaintiff's counsel that situations like the one faced
by Ms. Burrell raise important issues of access to justice.  The court should
not deny access to the courts with punishing costs orders such that they are
cowed from bringing simple motions for fear they will lose [as per
Moon v
Sher
(C.A.)] but this goes well beyond a simple lost motion.  This involves
a total abandonment of her obligations as a litigant and of her failure to
comply, or make any efforts to comply, with orders of the court.  While a
person has a right of access to the courts she must accept the accompanying
responsibility to comply with its rules and orders.

While I have no evidence whether Ms. Burrell had any
direct role in the failures that have led us to today, it is clear that her
solicitors have failed her in that regard.  I would point out that counsel
today, Mr. Agbakwa, has played no role in that failure.  He has made Herculean
efforts to comply in the last 2 weeks and he should be commended.  He has saved
an almost certain dismissal of this action.  However, the defendant is entitled
to compensation for the events prior to his involvement.  Whether Mr. Guiste or
Ms. Burrell pays these costs is between them to decide.

[
19
]

I did not order Mr. Guiste to pay the costs personally since such
order had not been sought and he had not been put on notice under rule
57.07(2). Although the costs order was made against the plaintiff alone I left
it up to Mr. Guiste and his client to decide which of them would pay the costs.
Clearly I had in mind that Mr. Guiste would “step up to the plate” and pay the
costs caused by his inattention to the file. These costs have never been paid
and the October 19, 2006 order is referred to as the “first unpaid costs
order”. That order forms part of the basis for the current motion before me to
dismiss the action for failure to pay costs.

THE MOTION TO AMEND AND THE SECOND
COSTS ORDER

[
20
]

With respect to the plaintiff’s motion to amend, I ordered on
October 19 on consent that the action against the Chief and one officer be
dismissed without costs, that certain defendants deliver affidavits or further
and better affidavits of documents and that any examination of the defendants
on the amendments if allowed be in writing. The plaintiff withdrew her request
for case management. With respect to the proposed amended statement of claim,
it was clear that the draft provided was insufficient and in any event the
plaintiff wanted to make further changes. I allowed the plaintiff to submit a redrafted
pleading. After further submissions in writing I allowed most of the amendments
by endorsement dated December 18, 2006.

[
21
]

Notwithstanding that the amendments were substantially allowed, I
denied the plaintiff costs of the motion and instead awarded costs of the
motion to the defendants payable within 30 days fixed in the sum of $1250. I
also awarded to the defendants their costs thrown away associated with the
amendments, payable in stages if and as the defendants amended their statement
of defence to the amended statement of claim, conducted examinations for
discovery on the amendments, responded to the plaintiff’s examinations
in-writing on the amendments and attended a second pre-trial. If all steps were
taken the costs thrown away would amount to $4900. The costs order of $1250
dated December 18, 2006 has never been paid and is referred to as the “second
unpaid costs order”.  That order also forms part of the basis for the current
motion before me to dismiss the action for failure to pay costs. The costs
thrown away are not yet payable other than $400 for delivering an amended
statement of defence.

[
22
]

My rationale for awarding costs of the amendment motion to the
defendants despite a measure of success by the plaintiff is set out in my
endorsement as follows:

The plaintiff is not entitled to her costs of this
motion for a number of reasons:

(a)

A motion for leave to
amend requires an indulgence by the court, particularly when it comes so late
in the action and after adjourning a second fixed trial date.

(b)

The motion was heard
only after the plaintiff had requested and obtained the adjournment of two
fixed trial dates because her solicitor was not ready for trial, one
adjournment being obtained with the defendants’ consent and one opposed. In
fact I would not allow the current amendment motion to proceed until it was
ascertained whether the plaintiff would be successful in obtaining the second
adjournment.

(c)

The amendment to plead
malicious prosecution after the statutory limitation period was not granted on
the basis asserted by the plaintiff, namely discoverability, but based on a
very generous reading of the original statement of claim by the court to allow
it to conclude that malicious prosecution had initially been asserted but
without all elements of the cause of action having been set out, an argument
not put forward by the plaintiff. It was reasonable for the defendants to
oppose and in fact were successful in opposing this amendment on the basis
asserted.

(d)

The amendment to refer
to racial profiling was conceded by the defendants after the plaintiff made it
clear that he was not pleading it as a separate tort but in support of the
cause of action based on charter breach.

(e)

It took the plaintiff
four tries over the course of this motion to get the amendments right. The
notice of motion dated August 8, 2006 had requested only two brief amendments
as set out in Mr. Guiste’s letter of July 6, 2006, namely to replace “assault”
with “battery” and to plead that the criminal charges against her were
dismissed. By the time the motion was first before me on October 19, 2006 a
brand new amended statement of claim had been drafted containing numerous
underlined changes. On October 19 I indicated there were deficiencies in the
draft and allowed the plaintiff to submit a new fresh as amended statement of
claim, which it did by letter dated November 6, 2006. Finally, as part of its written
submission in response to the defendants’ submissions on the amendments, the
plaintiff by letter dated December 4, 2006 submitted a new draft of paragraph
18.

(f)

The defendants were
successful in striking the reference to apartheid as scandalous in the
proffered amendments, although they were not successful in striking the
references to notoriety.

(g)

Leave to allow the
plaintiff to file a defence to counterclaim was required because the
plaintiff’s former counsel failed to file such defence upon receipt of the
counterclaim in December 2001 and no steps were taken to deliver a defence for
5 ½ years. The defendants did not oppose leave.

(h)

Although the plaintiff
obtained an order to examine the defendant officers on the amendments, she did
not obtain discovery of the chief of police which it sought in the notice of
motion and in fact on the third return date of the motion the plaintiff agreed
to a dismissal as against the chief. The defendants opposed a wide open further
examination of the defendant officers, but did not oppose their examination
with the restrictions set out in my October 19 order, namely that it be in
writing as ordered by Echlin J. and that it be restricted to examination on the
amendments and follow up questions on answers to undertakings.

(i)

The defendants
originally served an affidavit of documents only from the defendant Graham.
Although the plaintiff obtained an order to compel affidavits of documents from
the other defendants, there is no evidence of a demand being made prior to July
6, 2006 and the solicitors for the defendants began preparation of same upon
receipt thereof. Although a further and better affidavit of documents was
demanded from the defendant Graham, the plaintiff did not set out what
documents she believed were missing and the defendants advised there were no
further documents. The court however pointed out that Schedule B was not
particularized and an order was made accordingly.

(j)

The defendants were
successful in obtaining terms of allowing the amendments as requested, namely
further rights of discovery and costs thrown away.

[
23
]

The plaintiff never appealed nor sought leave to appeal either the
first unpaid costs order nor the second unpaid costs order.

THE CURRENT MOTION TO DISMISS AND
PLAINTIFF’S MOTIONS TO VARY

[
24
]

The defendant then brought this current motion to dismiss, or
alternatively stay, the action for failure to pay the first unpaid costs order.
The motion was served on December 11, 2006 and was returnable on January 29,
2007. Prior to the return date the second unpaid costs order became due and was
included in the grounds for relief. On January 23, 2007 the plaintiff served a
cross-motion to vary both the first and the second unpaid costs orders. Both
motions were returnable before Master Brott on January 29, 2007. There was a
disagreement whether the motions should be heard together or whether the
defendant’s motion proceed first. Master Brott ordered they be tried together,
adjourned to allow the defendants time to respond to the plaintiff’s
cross-motion to vary and referred both motions to me to be heard on March 8,
2007.

[
25
]

Mr. Guiste then advised by letters of February 25 and March 4 2007
that he wished to traverse the plaintiff’s cross-motion to a judge on the basis
that my orders were unconstitutional (denying to an impecunious plaintiff
access to the courts to seek a remedy under section 24 of the Charter) and that
I lacked jurisdiction to hear such motion. He had secured a date of April 27,
2007 before a judge, to be heard with a motion to vary the order of Echlin J. respecting
the deadline for delivering written interrogatories and an expert’s report,
both of which had been missed. He sought to adjourn the dismissal motion
scheduled for March 8 before me until after adjudication by a judge on the
motion to vary.

[
26
]

On the March 8, 2007 return date I opined that the motion to vary
should be heard by me as I made the original orders, but that the plaintiff had
the right to have it heard by a judge under rule 37.14(5)(b). I adjourned the dismissal
motion to June 7, 2007 to be heard after the motion to vary was heard by a
judge. I stated: “Notwithstanding that the plaintiff failed to appeal my orders
and notwithstanding that the grounds raised to vary appear not to fall within
rule 59.06, the plaintiff should have the opportunity to have the motion heard
before I hear the substantive relief of dismissing or staying the action for a
breach of an order that could conceivably be varied.” The plaintiff then
withdrew the cross-motion before me to vary the costs orders since the same relief
was requested in the new motion returnable April 27 before a judge.

[
27
]

On April 27 the plaintiff’s motion to vary my two costs orders and
the order of Echlin J. was heard by D. Brown J. who summarized the plaintiff’s
argument as follows in his endorsement dated April 30, 2007:

She deposed that she is impecunious and lives on
social assistance.  She cannot afford to pay the cost awards made by
Master Dash.  Those awards stand as a barrier between her and the
opportunity to have her day in court.  If the Defendants secure a
dismissal of her claim because she cannot pay the costs awards, she argued that
justice would not be done.  The plaintiff sought a remedy under section
24(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
.  She contended that for a judicial officer to
order costs on an interlocutory motion against an impecunious plaintiff when
the plaintiff has no realistic financial means of satisfying the order would
deprive the plaintiff of rights guaranteed to her under
section 7
of the
Charter
.
I understand that the plaintiff did not raise her
Charter
argument in
the course of making cost submissions to Master Dash.

[
28
]

The plaintiff alleged that my costs orders were wrong at law, that I
exercised my discretion in an incorrect manner and that I made certain factual
errors. Brown J. held that the plaintiff was essentially seeking to appeal
those orders, that an appeal “was clearly the proper route to follow” but the
plaintiff decided not to seek leave to appeal. Instead she elected to bring a
motion to vary under rule 59.06. He held that rule 59.06 had no application
because there was no accidental slip or omission, there was no change in
circumstance after the order was made and rule 59.06 did not give him
jurisdiction to correct mistakes she claimed were made by me. He therefore
dismissed the motion to vary without prejudice to “any right the plaintiff may
have under the rules of civil procedure to bring a motion before Master Dash to
vary those orders.”

[
29
]

Brown J. also refused to vary the order of Echlin J. respecting the
deadline to deliver written interrogatories and deliver an expert report. He
did not accept Mr. Guiste’s explanation of inadvertence and stated:

The records reveal to me that plaintiff’s counsel is
indifferent to any deadlines that are set, and he believes that this action can
proceed in a fashion and at a pace solely dictated by him.

I am total agreement with the above
observation of Brown J. He refused to deal with timetable issues in a piecemeal
fashion, but suggested that the plaintiff put together a comprehensive
timetable dealing with all further steps that need to be completed before
trial.

[
30
]

In a supplementary endorsement on June 8, 2007 dealing with costs of
the motion before him, Brown J. considered Mr. Guiste’s argument that the
plaintiff was impecunious and she should not be deprived of her day in court on
account of costs sanctions that she cannot pay. He noted that access to justice
goes hand in hand with fairness of justice to both parties. He stated as
follows with respect to the role of impecuniosity where, as in the case before
him, the impecunious litigant does not comply with court orders:

Even though the plaintiff may be a person of
modest or no means, that does not entitle her, or her counsel, to play by a
different set of procedural rules in asserting her claim.  In his order
dated October 2, 2006 Echlin J. required the plaintiff to perform several steps
in the litigation.  As I noted in paragraphs 22 through to 27 of my
endorsement, the plaintiff, or her counsel, failed to take the steps ordered or
meet the deadlines set.  Master Dash heard several procedural motions in
the summer and fall of 2006 and awarded costs against the plaintiff reflecting,
in part, the tenability of the positions taken by the plaintiff on those
motions.  If, having brought a claim, a party of modest means proceeds to
embark upon a procedural path that involves numerous unsuccessful interlocutory
motions, or seeks procedural relief from the justice system, but then fails to
comply with orders made by judicial officers, fairness dictates that the other
party should receive some compensation for the legal expense to which it has
been put, notwithstanding the limited resources of the other party.  A
person’s modest financial position cannot serve as an excuse to play by a
different set of procedural rules.

In the result Brown J. ordered costs of
$2500 payable by the plaintiff by July 15, however if she moved to have the
action case managed by June 28 the costs would be to the defendants in the
cause.

[
31
]

The defendant’s motion to dismiss then came back on before me on
June 7, 2007. Mr. Guiste was excused to attend a continuing trial and the
motion did not proceed. Despite objections from the defendant, the motion was
adjourned to July 23, 2007 with a deadline for responding material and
cross-examination.

[
32
]

On June 20 the plaintiff served another cross-motion returnable
before me on July 23, 2007. The motion was to vary my two costs orders and to
bring the action into case management. The relief requested on the motion to
vary was identical to that which was originally before me on March 8, 2007 and
withdrawn and identical to the motion to vary that was argued before Brown J.
on April 27, 2007 and dismissed. The plaintiff relied on the affidavit of Ms.
Burrell filed on the earlier motion. The plaintiff averred that she was
disabled as a result of injuries suffered at the hands of the defendant
officers, that her sole sources of income were two disability pensions totalling
$542.70 per month and that her fixed monthly expenses totalled $440. She stated
she did not have the means to pay the costs orders but was content that they be
paid out of any award for costs she received at the end of this litigation.

[
33
]

On July 23, 2007 both the defendant’s motion to dismiss for failure
to comply with the costs orders and the plaintiff’s motion to vary the costs
orders came before me. I first heard the plaintiff’s cross-motion to vary the
costs orders. I dismissed the motion for the same reasons as Brown J. – that
there were no grounds under rule 59.06 to vary the order and that the proper
remedy was to seek leave to appeal the costs rulings, but the plaintiff has
never sought leave to appeal. Mr. Guiste argued that I had not taken into
account the plaintiff’s specific financial circumstances, but as can be seen
from my endorsement of October 19, 2006 I considered the plaintiff’s
impecuniosity, but decided that it should not shield her from costs sanctions when
she had totally abandoned her obligations as litigant. It was not necessary for
me to know the exact amount of her income and expenses as I had accepted at the
time that she was impecunious and on social assistance. I also noted that the
plaintiff had argued her impecuniosity on the original motion before me on
October 19, 2006 when costs were awarded, had withdrawn her motion to vary
before me on March 8, 2007 and chose to argue the variation before Brown J. on
April 27. I determined that the plaintiff was attempting a third kick at the
same can. Time then ran out and I adjourned the defendant’s motion to dismiss
and the plaintiff’s request for case management to September 25, 2007.

[
34
]

On September 25, 2007 the defendant’s motion to dismiss was finally
argued. It was the fifth time the parties had appeared on the dismissal motion
since the first attendance on January 29, 2007. I reserved my decision.

THE ROLE OF IMPECUNIOSITY IN COSTS
AWARDS AND DISMISSAL MOTIONS

[
35
]

The defendants rely on rules 57.03(2) and 60.12 which provide:

57.03
(1)
On the hearing of a
contested motion, unless the court is satisfied that a different order would be
more just, the court shall,

(a) fix the costs of the motion and order them to be paid within 30 days…

(2)
Where a party fails to pay the
costs of a motion as required under subrule (1), the court              may
dismiss or stay the party’s proceeding, strike out the party’s defence or make
such other order as is just.

60.12
Where a party fails to comply with an
interlocutory order, the court may, in addition to any other sanction provided
by these rules,

(a)
stay the party’s proceeding;

(b)
dismiss the party’s proceeding or strike out the party’s defence; or

(c)
make such other order as is just.

[
36
]

Costs are a matter within the discretion of the judge or master
hearing a motion and the court may determine by whom and to what extent costs
shall be paid.
[2]

The court is to take into account the factors under rule 57.01
[3]
and make a costs award that is
fair and reasonable in the circumstances. The normal rule is that costs of a
contested motion are payable by the losing party to the winning party, although
the fact that a party is successful does not prevent an award of costs against
the winning party.
[4]

In accordance with rule 57.03(1) the presumptive rule is that costs are fixed
by the motions judge or master and payable within 30 days, although a different
order may be made if more just.

[
37
]

In this case, both the first unpaid costs order and the second
unpaid costs order were ordered to be paid by the plaintiff to the defendant
within 30 days from the date of the order and in both cases the costs awarded
were not paid within 30 days or at all. This is not a motion to vary those
orders. That motion has already been heard twice and dismissed both times.
Under rule 57.03(2) the court may dismiss or stay a party’s action if that
party fails to pay the costs awarded on a motion and under rule 60.12 the court
may stay or dismiss the action of a party who fails to comply with an
interlocutory order of the court. Both rules however also provide that in lieu
of dismissing or staying the action of the party who has failed to comply, the
court may make “such other order as is just.”

[
38
]

Mr. Guiste argues that his client, who is impecunious, cannot pay
the costs awarded and that if I dismiss her action as a result, she will be
denied access to the courts. He suggests it would be more just to allow the
action to continue and set off the costs awards against any costs or damages
awarded to the plaintiff in this action after final disposition thereof.
Although this would have the same effect as a variation, relief already sought
and rejected, I must consider whether it would be more just to allow the action
to proceed rather than dismissing the action or staying the action until the
costs are paid.

[
39
]

Under rule 57.01(1) one of the factors the court may consider in
awarding costs is “any other matter relevant to the issue of costs.”
[5]
Courts have determined that a
party’s impecuniosity or financial circumstances may be considered under this
provision in awarding costs.
[6]

The dilemma is this: If an award of costs were made that a party has no means
to satisfy, and the action is dismissed or stayed as a result, the party would
be denied access to our civil courts and the action would never be heard on its
merits. On the other hand, a party should not be able to set up his or her
impecunious circumstances as a shield against costs sanctions when he has
failed to comply with the rules and orders of the court.

[
40
]

A number of court decisions have addressed the need to compel
parties to comply with court orders and the unfairness that would result if a
party who fails to comply with court orders were allowed to set up
impecuniosity as a shield against costs sanctions. For example:

(a)

For orders of the court
to have any meaning they must be enforced…[A] party should not be able to set
up his own impecuniosity as a shield against costs sanctions. To allow that
would mean that a plaintiff could bring, resist, or appeal motions with no fear
of consequences, and would emasculate the powers provided in rules 57.03(2) and
60.12.
[7]

(b)

If this court’s rules
are to be taken seriously by anybody, they must be enforced.
[8]

(c)

The court if it fails
to act becomes but a paper tiger.
[9]

(d)

There will be
situations where a party’s position ought to be determined for procedural
reasons arising from the failure of that party to abide by orders made by the
court. If it were the case that the merits of the matter always had to be
determined before such remedies could be imposed, there would be little room
for the effective application of either of these rules.
[10]

(e)

Because of the importance
of avoiding a situation in which litigants without means could ignore the rules
of the court, the trial judge acted reasonably in refusing to take into account
the impecuniosity of the plaintiff.
[11]

(f)

Even if I were
persuaded that the Appellant/Plaintiff is impoverished and without assets,
which I am not, there would be good reason not to allow the appeal to proceed
when costs have not been paid. Not only would that shift the economic burden of
the proceedings to which the order relates to the Respondent/Defendant contrary
to the costs principles on which it was based, it would also allow the
Appellant/Plaintiff to continue court proceedings without complying with the
courts orders.
[12]

(g)

[If the plaintiff] were
permitted to continue without complying with the order, the conduct would go
unsanctioned and the court would lose all pretence of control over the party's
conduct.
[13]

(h)

It would be most unfair
if the plaintiff could refuse to answer proper questions at a discovery and
could oppose and bring motions with no possible sanction except that at the end
of the action she may, if she is successful in the action, be required to set
off the costs of those motions against any award she receives… To accede to the
plaintiff’s request would give her carte blanche to continue to ignore the
rules and orders of the court and take unsupportable steps in this action
without fear of consequences, yet cause the defendants to continue to incur
substantial costs while they enforce their rights to proper discovery and move
this proceeding toward trial.
[14]

(i)

While there is a right
of Canadians to have access to our courts, there is an accompanying
responsibility to abide by the rules of civil procedure and to comply with
orders of the court. When costs orders are made, they must be complied with or
orders of the court lose their legitimacy.
[15]

(j)

There may be situations
where a clearly meritorious case should not be dismissed against an impecunious
plaintiff for failing to pay interlocutory costs orders, but given the need of
the court to retain control over its processes and the legitimacy of its
orders, such situations should be the exception and not the norm.
[16]

(k)

These
defendants have had these very serious allegations hanging over their heads for
years. Allowing the action to continue when costs and undertakings are
outstanding would give carte blanche to the plaintiff to ignore orders of the
court while causing the defendants to continue to incur significant costs.
[17]

(l)

I have
concluded from reviewing the authorities that obstructionism and unreasonable
conduct leading to unnecessary motions is generally visited with an order for
immediate payment of the costs resulting from that conduct and impecuniosity of
the party liable to pay such costs does not constitute a shield. Conversely,
unreasonable conduct should not be rewarded by delaying payments of such costs
just because of impecuniosity.
[18]

(m)

Even though the plaintiff may be a person of
modest or no means, that does not entitle her, or her counsel, to play by a
different set of procedural rules in asserting her claim…If, having brought a
claim, a party of modest means proceeds to embark upon a procedural path that
involves numerous unsuccessful interlocutory motions, or seeks procedural
relief from the justice system, but then fails to comply with orders made by
judicial officers, fairness dictates that the other party should receive some
compensation for the legal expense to which it has been put, notwithstanding
the limited resources of the other party.  A person’s modest financial
position cannot serve as an excuse to play by a different set of procedural
rules.
[19]

(n)

The only issue
raised by him on the appeal was whether the learned trial judge, knowing of the
alleged impecuniosity of the plaintiff, should have required the costs to be
paid by the plaintiff within 15 days, and that the action be dismissed, if the
costs were not paid. The position taken before us on behalf of the plaintiff
was that those costs should have been made payable in any event of the cause,
in which event they would not have been payable until completion of the
trial….Because of the importance of avoiding a situation in which litigants
without means can ignore the rules of the court with impunity, and the
distastefulness of creating a rule incapable of consistent application, the learned
trial judge in the case at bar, in my opinion, acted reasonably in refusing to
take into account the impecuniosity of the plaintiff. The Orders fell squarely
within his discretionary power.
[20]

[
41
]

The plaintiff relies heavily on the costs decision of Lane J. in
Walsh
v. 1124660 Ontario Limited
,
[21]

following a lengthy trial in which Mr. Guiste was counsel for the plaintiff who
had sued a Tim Horton’s franchise where she had worked and the police. Ms.
Walsh was caught on videotape pocketing money and was fired and charged with
theft, a charge subsequently withdrawn by the police. After a lengthy jury
trial the action was dismissed against all defendants, a decision that Lane J.
summarized as: “In essence the jury found her guilty of theft.”

[
42
]

Lane J. then considered the issue of costs as against the plaintiff.
He considered the decision on
Myers

v. Toronto Police
where the Divisional Court stated (emphasis mine):

Because of the
importance of avoiding a situation in which litigants without means can ignore
the rules of the court with impunity, and the distastefulness of creating a
rule incapable of consistent application, the learned trial judge in the case
at bar, in my opinion, acted reasonably in refusing to take into account the
impecuniosity of the plaintiff.
The orders fell squarely within his
discretionary power.
[22]

Lane J. noted
: “
The reasoning in
Myers
in the

Divisional Court
is legally persuasive, as the statement of an appellate
level court on the very issue before me. I note that it has been followed by a
number of my colleagues.”
[23]

[
43
]

Lane J. concluded from the above quote from
Myers
as follows:
“From this passage it can be seen, despite the strong
language in support of the ruling of the trial judge, that the case does not
lay down any principle that it would be wrong for a judge to consider
impecuniosity in this context. It puts the matter ‘squarely within his
discretionary power’”.
[24]

He added:

In my opinion, impecuniosity falls within Rule 57.01:
"any other matter relevant to the question of costs." Whether to
consider it as a factor in any particular case remains a matter within the
discretion of the judge.
[25]

Lane J. thus
recognized that it is within the discretion of the judge or master to consider
impecuniosity as a factor in the award of costs, and if so to what extent.

[
44
]

In
Walsh
, Lane J. did not order costs against the impecunious
plaintiff, concluding:

The plaintiff is unable to pay and will
likely remain so as she lacks both skills and the time and money to acquire
them so long as she must care for her children on public support. She incurred
this potential liability in the pursuit of the restoration of her employment
and her reputation after being dismissed. She has been unsuccessful after a
proceeding which no one could have imagined would cost what it did. A costs
order against her in the amounts sought, or indeed in any lesser, but
significant amount, would have no practical utility to the defendants, but
would send a message which would deter others, who may have better cases, from
pursuing a remedy because of the disastrous impact of costs if they lose the
case. The courts exist to hear the complaints of the people. It is not in the
public interest to deter the people from using their own courts for fear of the
costs consequences if they lose the case.
[26]

Mr. Guiste suggests that based on this
reasoning, Ms. Burrell should not lose her rights to pursue her actions because
of unpaid costs orders she cannot afford to pay.

[
45
]

Lane J. however was dealing with costs at the conclusion of a trial
and not on an interlocutory motion. In fact Lane J. recognized the distinction
by stating that after trial there is no further conduct of the plaintiff to
deter, as would be the case at an interlocutory stage. In my view the nub of
his decision is set out in the following passage (emphasis mine):

19
Clearly, I
must take into consideration the warning given
in
Myers

not to create a situation permitting litigants without means to thumb their
noses at the court. Such situations do occur and when one recognizes the symptoms,
there are remedies which can be applied which are not confined to costs. In any
event, for the truly impecunious, who know they will never have to pay, my
experience is that costs are not the most effective weapon.
When a party
refuses to do an act, we can, with suitable warnings, dismiss his case or
strike her defence. Such cases are best dealt with on a case by case basis.

Immediate payment of costs is a wonderful weapon when it is also a fair one,
but the judge's discretion is wide enough to enable the creation of a penalty
for non-compliance that is fair in the circumstances.

20
In the
present case, unlike
Myers
, we are dealing with
costs after the trial is over, so no issue of on-going non-compliance with
orders, or defying the court exists. There is no future conduct of this
plaintiff to deter.

The simple question is whether there can be a consideration of the paying
party's means in considering the disposition of costs. In my opinion, the
answer to this question must be yes where impecuniosity is demonstrated…
Whether to consider it as a factor in any particular case remains a matter
within the discretion of the judge.
[27]

[
46
]

It is clear from the above passages that Lane J. acknowledged that
costs against an impecunious litigant may be justified to deter future conduct
when there had been non-compliance with court orders and that dismissal of an
action may be justified where a party refuses to comply with orders after
suitable warnings. It is a matter within the court’s discretion to make such
determination as is just in all the circumstances.

[
47
]

In the recent decision of
Christian Jew Foundation v. Christian
Jew Outreach
[28]

Perell J. undertook “
an analysis of the role of impecuniosity as a factor in the
court's discretion to award costs.”
[29]
In that case the defendants sought leave to appeal an award of
costs of $29,974 made by Master Sproat following a productions and refusals
motion. Leave to appeal was sought partly on the basis that the defendants were
impecunious and unable to pay, thus exposing them to a motion to strike their
statement of defence and counterclaim under rules 57.03(2) and 60.12. They
argued in their factum that “justice is subverted if [the defendants] never get
an opportunity to go to trial.” They objected to the requirement that the costs
be payable within 30 days as ordered and submitted they should instead be paid
in any event of the cause. This is similar to the arguments made by Mr. Guiste
on the motions to vary before both Brown J. and myself. Perell J. denied leave
to appeal and held that if he had granted leave he would have dismissed the
appeal on its merits and refused to vary the costs order of Master Sproat.

[
48
]

Perell J. first reviews two lines of cases that considers whether impecuniosity
may be a relevant factor to consider in the award and enforcement of costs.

61
I begin
this exploration by noting that there are authorities that support the
proposition that a party's impecuniosity is not a relevant factor in the
exercise of a court's discretion in awarding or enforcing costs awards. In
particular, impecuniosity will not insulate a party from liability of costs
otherwise payable and impecuniosity cannot be used as a justification for
failure to obey a court's orders:
[case citations]

62
The policy
rationales behind this line of authority are that: (a) a rule based on
impecuniosity would present problems of interpretation, evidence, and
application and such a rule would be undesirable; (b) and the courts would
become powerless to control an impecunious party who could bring and defend
motions without fear of any sanction for irresponsibly bringing or resisting
interlocutory motions, and, therefore, impecuniosity should not be a factor in
awarding or enforcing costs awards.

…

64
There are,
however, authorities that support the proposition that impecuniosity is a
relevant factor and may be considered in awarding and in enforcing costs awards
including determining when the costs should be payable:
[case citations]

65
The policy
rationale behind this competing line of cases that access to justice is a
necessary and desirable attribute of the administration of justice and access
to justice may be thwarted if the effect of a party's impecuniosity is ignored
when the court exercises its discretion to award or enforce a costs award.
[30]

[
49
]

Perell J. then considered the decision of Blair J.A. in
Larabie
v. Montfils
[31]

where the plaintiff was appealing an order dismissing his action as an abuse of
process and the defendants moved for security for costs because of unpaid costs
orders. Blair J.A. determined that the plaintiff was impecunious and an order
for security for costs would deprive him of adjudication on the merits. He
recited the well-known rule in security for costs cases that “
courts are reluctant to
deprive a worthy but impecunious litigant of the opportunity to have his or her
claim adjudicated when it is not plainly devoid of merit”.
[32]
Blair J.A. weighed
the competing factors and interests, including the proposition that “litigants
are not free to ignore or flout orders of the court awarding costs against
them” and decided to “exercise my discretion” and allow the appeal to proceed
without posting security.
[33]

[
50
]

Perell J. opined that the approach by Blair J. was the preferable
one and stated:

In most cases, impecuniosity will not be a
factor; however, as I understand Justice Blair's more flexible approach, in the
exercise of its discretion, a court can probe the circumstances and assess,
what might be called "the procedural good faith" of the party using
impecuniosity as his or her excuse for failing to comply with a court order,
including a failure to pay costs. Is the person using impecuniosity as a means
to avoid his or her responsibilities or in good faith as an apology or
explanation for failing to do so?
[34]

He supported this by the following
passage from
Heu v. Forder Estate
:

There may be situations where a clearly
meritorious case should not be dismissed against an impecunious plaintiff for
failing to pay interlocutory costs orders, but given the need of the court to
retain control over its process and the legitimacy of its orders, such
situations should be the exception and not the norm.
[35]

[
51
]

Perell J. decided that because Master Sproat had not accepted that
the plaintiffs were impecunious, it was not necessary for her to exercise her
discretion, but even if impecuniosity had been proven, Master Sproat’s exercise
of discretion to order payment of costs within 30 days would not have been
clearly wrong.
[36]

[
52
]

Although the matter before Perell J. had not yet reached the stage
where a dismissal or stay was sought based on failure to pay the costs award
(as it is in the matter before me), he had this to say:

[I]t remains to be seen whether the
Foundation and Mr. Hedrick will move and rely on rules 57.03(2) or 60.12 to
stay the counterclaim or strike out the party's defence; in that event,

following
Larabie v. Montfils
, supra
, the court
retains the discretion to permit the defence and counterclaim to proceed.

[
53
]

Therefore, when faced with a motion to dismiss or stay an action
brought by an impecunious plaintiff who has not paid costs awarded on an
interlocutory motion, the court retains a discretion to either dismiss or stay
the action or allow it to proceed, in other words to “make such order as is
just.”

[
54
]

The cases to which I have referred lead me to conclude that the
court has a discretion to take into account the impecuniosity of a litigant in
an award of costs and on a motion to dismiss for failure to pay those costs. The
court should consider as a relevant factor in the exercise of its discretion
the effect on access to justice if costs are sought to be awarded or enforced
against an impecunious litigant, but the court is free to then it give it
whatever weight it deems appropriate in all of the circumstances, including no
weight. Furthermore, although impecuniosity is a relevant factor, it is only
one factor. There is not only one party involved in the action – the defendant
has rights as well which the court must take into account. It is unfair that
the defendants continue to incur substantial costs in compelling the plaintiff
to comply with her production and discovery obligations and with court orders, when
that plaintiff could, in the absence of sanctions, have carte blanche to ignore
orders of the court and to bring, resist and appeal motions with impunity, with
no fear of costs consequences by simply pleading impecuniosity at every turn.
The court must also take into account the interest of the court in ensuring
that its rules and orders are not ignored and retaining some measure of control
over a party’s conduct. There must be fairness and a balancing of interests,
but clearly a person’s modest means cannot serve as an excuse to play by a
different set of procedural rules and ignore orders of the court and the rules
of court with impunity. Unreasonable conduct should not be rewarded by denying
costs to the innocent defendant or by deferring payment until after trial.

[
55
]

Among the factors the court should consider in determining what
result is just on a motion to dismiss an action against an impecunious litigant
for failure to pay a costs award, are the circumstances that led up to the
award of costs. For example, were the costs awarded, notwithstanding the
plaintiff’s impecuniosity, to deter bad behaviour, such as the flouting of the
rules or orders of the court, or were they simply an award of costs against a
losing party to a motion brought or resisted in good faith and on reasonable
grounds? Perell J. stated in
Christian Jew Foundation
that the court
should “probe the circumstances and assess…the procedural good faith of the
party using impecuniosity as his or her excuse for failing to comply with a
court order” and suggested the court ask: “
Is the person using impecuniosity as a means to avoid his
or her responsibilities or in good faith as an apology or explanation for
failing to do so?”
[37]

Clearly, there is a more compelling case for not
allowing a litigant to avoid a dismissal or stay of the action for failure to
pay costs when the litigant’s behaviour that led to the costs award involved
flouting orders of the court and ignoring the rules of the very court to which
they claim a right of access.

CONCLUSION

[
56
]

In the matter before me, the first unpaid costs
award was made on October 19, 2006 in the following circumstances. The
plaintiff had not answered her undertakings since her discovery in December
2004. Mr. Guiste had done nothing to answer the undertakings from the time he
took possession of the file in December 2005. Initially he believed all
undertakings were answered based on an assurance from Ms. Lewis, the former
solicitor. That assumption was dispelled the next month when he was served with
a motion to enforce undertakings on January 4, 2006. All of the undertakings were
set out in a chart in the motion record. Nonetheless, he took steps whatsoever even
to look at the file to confirm whether the undertakings were in fact outstanding,
let alone attend to answering them. He
promised on several occasions to provide the answers, but
took no steps to do so. He then

consented to the order before Master Clark on June 27, 2006 to answer specified
undertakings by August 3, 2006, despite his alleged understanding that all
undertakings were satisfied. Again he took no steps whatsoever to comply with
that order, except to sign some authorizations that the defendant provided.
When the defendants’ motion to dismiss the action for failure to comply with
the order of Master Clark came before me on August 11, 2006, Mr. Guiste had
still made absolutely no attempts to comply. He continued to assert that there
were no outstanding undertakings, yet he had taken no steps to review the file
to confirm this. I adjourned to allow the plaintiff to comply with the
undertakings or to put in responding material to show they had been answered.
On the return date of September 28, still nothing had been done to comply nor
was any evidence proffered to demonstrate that the undertakings were answered
(other than signing the authorizations).

[
57
]

I held at that time that the plaintiff (or more
likely Mr. Guiste) had shown a cavalier attitude to her responsibilities as a
litigant and given the lack of any attempt to comply with undertakings given
and with the order of Master Clark I would have been justified in dismissing
the action. Nonetheless I acknowledged that dismissal was an extreme remedy and
I gave the plaintiff yet a further opportunity to comply. Finally Mr. Agbakwa
took the matter in hand and prior to the October 19 return date substantially
complied with the undertakings. In awarding costs I accepted and considered the
plaintiff’s impecuniosity and her rights of access to justice, however I held
that this was not a matter of simply losing a motion, but rather
“this involves a total abandonment of her obligations as a litigant
and of her failure to comply, or make any efforts to comply, with orders of the
court.” I am in complete agreement with the observation of Brown J. on the
first motion to vary the costs awards when he stated: “Plaintiff’s counsel is indifferent to any deadlines that are set, and
he believes that this action can proceed in a fashion and at a pace solely
dictated by him.” I agree with
Ms. Kotsopoulos who argued that this motion is not so much about access to
justice, but is about the failure of Mr. Guiste to litigate this action
reasonably, to obey orders of the court and to properly utilize and comply with
the rules of the court.

[
58
]

Throughout, the defendants were forced to incur
substantial expense to compel the plaintiff to comply with her discovery
obligations and with the order of the court.
There is a reasonable expectation that the defaulting plaintiff will
bear at least a portion of those costs.

[
59
]

There can be no reasonable excuse for failing to take any steps to
comply with undertakings and a consent order of the court or for Mr. Guiste failing
to give the file any attention whatsoever in the ten months since he took
possession of it. Mr. Guiste pleads for his client’s right of access to the
court, yet refuses to accept the accompanying responsibility for complying with
its rules and orders. There is no evidence that the plaintiff’s impecuniosity
was in any way responsible for her failure to answer undertakings or to comply
with the order of Master Clark. In no way could the behaviour of the plaintiff
and her counsel be considered as a good faith explanation for failing to
comply. Impecuniosity was clearly raised solely to avoid her responsibilities
as a litigant and the consequences of breaching those responsibilities. In no
manner could this be considered a situation where costs were being awarded
against an impecunious party who lost a motion that was
resisted in good faith on reasonable grounds.

[
60
]

Even Mr. Guiste, when pressed to articulate whether costs should
ever be awarded against an impecunious litigant, stated that any person who
abused the rules or made a mockery of the judicial process should be punished
with costs, but they should be fair and reasonable. In my view that standard is
too high, but even if I were to consider Mr. Guiste’s suggestion, I would find
it difficult to understand how any reasonable person could fail to view the
actions of the plaintiff or her solicitors as abusing the rules and making a
mockery of the courts. The costs awarded were fair and reasonable and were
considerably less than the actual costs expended by the defendants in enforcing
the plaintiff’s discovery obligations.

[
61
]

I asked Mr. Guiste if he personally accepts any responsibility for
the events that led to the costs order. Mr. Guiste blames everything that has
gone wrong in this file on others. In particular he continues to blame Ms.
Lewis for the misinformation given in November 2005 when he took over the file
that undertakings were answered. He does not accept that his failure to do
anything to engage the file from the time he took it over in November 2005 and
from the time he received a detailed list of undertakings in January 2006 or
that his consenting to an order to answer undertakings in June 2006 and doing
nothing to comply until his back was against the wall following three
attendances on a motion to dismiss in October 2006 had anything to do with the
costs order that was made.

[
62
]

Although I made the award against the plaintiff personally and not
against Mr. Guiste, and although I was aware that the plaintiff might be unable
to pay the $5000 costs awarded within 30 days, I noted: “While I have no evidence whether Ms. Burrell had any direct role in
the failures that have led us to today, it is clear that her solicitors have
failed her in that regard...Whether Mr. Guiste or Ms. Burrell pay these costs
is between them to decide.” The message was loud and clear. If Mr. Guiste was
responsible for the events that led up to the award of costs, he should “step
up to the plate” and pay them so that the action would not be dismissed.
However, neither Ms. Burrell nor Mr. Guiste has paid the costs, although I am
advised that approximately $300 was paid prior to the March 8, 2007 appearance.
Although the plaintiff offered to make payments over time, there was never a
concrete proposal in that regard. Although Mr. Guiste complains that Mr.
Mazzuca did not seek his client’s instructions for a payment schedule, one was
never proposed and the matter not further pursued by Mr. Guiste.

[
63
]

In my view a dismissal order would be just in the circumstances,
despite the plaintiff’s impecuniosity. When orders of the court are cavalierly ignored,
when a litigant continuously fails to comply with her obligations as a litigant
and then fails to abide by the costs consequences attendant upon that
behaviour, the court is justified in bringing some finality to the action.
However, dismissal is a drastic remedy and in my view it is more appropriate to
stay the action to give the plaintiff or Mr. Guiste one last opportunity to pay
the costs in order that the action may proceed. As I stated in
Heu v. Forder
,
much of which is applicable to the matter before me at this time:

Notwithstanding that a dismissal would be appropriate
I also acknowledge that a dismissal is an extreme remedy, to be applied as a
last resort. While the plaintiff’s failure to pay the costs threatens the
court’s ability to enforce its own orders, and perhaps indicates an
unwillingness of the plaintiff to accept that she should be responsible for her
conduct that has resulted in the defendants incurring costs…[i]t would be just
to allow the plaintiff one final opportunity to pay her outstanding costs
awards, as well as costs of this motion. The defendants, however, should not be
required to continue to expend even more funds in the defence of this action
until the costs it has already incurred as a result of the plaintiff’s conduct,
as reflected in costs orders made to date, are first paid.
[38]

To assure, however, that the plaintiff pays costs of
interlocutory motions awarded against her during the course of the proceeding,
the order that in my view is most just is to stay the action until the
interlocutory cost awards have been paid. In my view that will drive home to
the plaintiff that she does not have a “free ride” and that there is a price to
pay when she refuses to answer proper questions, unreasonably opposes proper
motions or brings her own motions which are unsuccessful. As stated by Eberhard
J. in
Stacey
, supra, the plaintiff “should be given the opportunity, now
that the stakes have been made clear, to comply with the cost order in order to
continue to adjudication on the merits.”
[39]

If the costs are not paid and the stay lifted within
six months the defendants may again move to dismiss the action, since these
doctors cannot have these allegation hanging over their heads indefinitely. I
concur with Eberhard J. who stated, “a stay until such time as the…Plaintiff
chooses to comply with the cost order is too open-ended. The issues should be
brought to adjudication in the time frame fixed or be terminated.”
[40]

[
64
]

In
Heu v. Forder
I allowed six months to pay before I would
entertain a dismissal. I appreciate that it is extremely unlikely the plaintiff
will be in any better financial circumstances in six months than she is now.
Realistically, the only way that the stay will be lifted and a dismissal avoided
is for Mr. Guiste to pay the costs for which he is responsible. This should not
take more than six months if Mr. Guiste accepts this responsibility. I wish to
make it clear that if the costs are not paid in that time the action will be
dismissed barring the most exceptional of circumstances.

[
65
]

With respect to the second unpaid costs order arising out of the
motion to amend, I am of the view that those costs arose not because of the
plaintiff or Mr. Guiste failing to comply with orders of the court or flouting
her obligations as litigant. They were not far off the mark however given the
lateness in serving a motion to amend and adjourning two trial dates in the
process because the pleadings were not yet in order and Mr. Guiste was not
ready for trial. Although the costs of the motion to amend, as well as the
costs thrown away resulting from the amendments, were properly made as against
the plaintiff for reasons set out earlier in this endorsement, the motion was
reasonable and necessary in order to bring the pleadings in line with the
plaintiff’s view of the action, notwithstanding that it could have been made
much earlier. I would not require that these costs be paid in order to lift the
stay. Once the balance of the first unpaid costs order of $5000 is paid the
stay may be lifted and the plaintiff will be entitled to proceed with her
action.

[
66
]

If the stay is lifted, I will grant the plaintiff’s motion to
transfer the action into case management. As stated both by Brown J. and
myself, the action cries out for case management to get it back on the rails.
Case management is appropriate given the plaintiff’s inattention in moving the
action forward and chronic obstruction in complying with her discovery
obligations. I warn the plaintiff however that once the action is case managed,
a timetable will be set forthwith for the balance of the litigation events to
make the action trial ready in an expedited time frame. The court will not
abide the plaintiff breaching the timetable or seeking further extensions. I
also put the plaintiff on notice that despite allowing the action to proceed
despite non-payment of the December 18, 2006 costs order, she should not expect
similar leniency if future cost awards become necessary.

ORDER

[
67
]

I order as follows:

(1)

This action is stayed.

(2)

The stay may be lifted on motion by the plaintiff after payment of
the balance owing on the costs order made on October 19, 2006 together with
interest thereon pursuant to the Courts of Justice Act.

(3)

If the stay is lifted, the action may proceed notwithstanding
non-payment of the costs or the costs thrown away as ordered on December 18,
2006. The plaintiff will pay those costs to the defendants after final
disposition of the action in any event of the cause.

(4)

If the stay is lifted, this action will be subject to case
management.

(5)

If the stay is not lifted within six months of the date this
endorsement is released, the defendants may move to dismiss the action

COSTS

[
68
]

I will accept brief written submissions from the defendants with
respect to costs of this motion within 10 days and any responding submissions
from the plaintiff within seven days of receipt of defendants’ submissions. Any
party seeking costs must include a Costs Outline (Form 57B) and supporting
dockets.
